passages.text: 3 Randomized prior functions for deep ensembles

Section 2 motivates the need for effective uncertainty estimates in deep RL. We note that crucial failure cases of several popular approaches can arise even with simple linear models. As a result, we take a moment to review the setting of Bayesian linear regression. Let θ ∈ ℝ d \theta\in\mathds{R}^{d} with prior N ⁡ ( θ ¯ , λ ​ I ) N(\overline{\theta},\lambda I) and data 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 n \mathcal{D}=\left\{(x_{i},y_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{n} for x i ∈ ℝ d x_{i}\in\mathds{R}^{d} and y i = θ T ​ x i + ϵ i y_{i}=\theta^{T}x_{i}+\epsilon_{i} with ϵ i ∼ N ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \epsilon_{i}\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}) iid. Then, conditioned on 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , the posterior for θ \theta is Gaussian:

𝔼 ⁡ [ θ ∣ 𝒟 ] = ( 1 σ 2 ​ X T ​ X + 1 λ ​ I ) − 1 ​ ( 1 σ 2 ​ X T ​ y + 1 λ ​ θ ¯ ) , Cov ⁡ [ θ ∣ 𝒟 ] = ( 1 σ 2 ​ X T ​ X + 1 λ ​ I ) − 1 . \mathds{E}\left[\theta\mid\mathcal{D}\right]=\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}X^{T}X+\frac{1}{\lambda}I\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}X^{T}y+\frac{1}{\lambda}\overline{\theta}\right),\quad{\rm Cov}\left[\theta\mid\mathcal{D}\right]=\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}X^{T}X+\frac{1}{\lambda}I\right)^{-1}. (3)

Equation ( 3 ) relies on Gaussian conjugacy and linear models, which cannot easily be extended to deep neural networks. The following result shows that we can replace this analytical result with a simple computational procedure.

Then the either of the following optimization problems generate a sample θ | 𝒟 \theta\mid\mathcal{D} according to ( 3 ):

arg ​ min θ ∑ i = 1 n ∥ y ~ i − f θ ( x i ) ∥ 2 2 + σ 2 λ ∥ θ ~ − θ ∥ 2 2 , \displaystyle\argmin_{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\tilde{y}_{i}-f_{\theta}(x_{i})\|^{2}_{2}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\lambda}\|\tilde{\theta}-\theta\|^{2}_{2}, (4) θ ~ + arg ​ min θ ∑ i = 1 n ∥ y ~ i − ( f θ ~ + f θ ) ( x i ) ∥ 2 2 + σ 2 λ ∥ θ ∥ 2 2 . \displaystyle\tilde{\theta}+\argmin_{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\tilde{y}_{i}-\left(f_{\tilde{\theta}}+f_{\theta}\right)(x_{i})\|^{2}_{2}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\lambda}\|\theta\|^{2}_{2}. (5)
To prove ( 4 ) note that the solution is Gaussian and then match moments; equation ( 5 ) then follows by relabeling [ 49 ] . ∎

Lemma 3 is revealing since it allows us to view Bayesian regression through a purely computational lens: ‘generate posterior samples by training on noisy versions of the data, together with some random regularization’. Even for nonlinear f θ f_{\theta} , we can still compute ( 4 ) or ( 5 ). Although the resultant f θ f_{\theta} will no longer be an exact posterior, at least it passes the ‘sanity check’ in this simple linear setting (unlike the approaches of Section 2 ). We argue this method is quite intuitive: the perturbed data 𝒟 ~ = { ( x i , y ~ i ) } i = 1 n \tilde{\mathcal{D}}=\{(x_{i},\tilde{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} is generated according to the estimated noise process ϵ t \epsilon_{t} and the sample θ ~ \tilde{\theta} is drawn from prior beliefs. Intuitively ( 4 ) says to fit to 𝒟 ~ \tilde{\mathcal{D}} and regularize weights to a prior sample of weights θ ~ \tilde{\theta} ; ( 5 ) says to generate a prior function f θ ~ f_{\tilde{\theta}} and then fit an additive term to noisy data 𝒟 ~ \tilde{\mathcal{D}} with regularized complexity.

This paper explores the performance of each of these methods for uncertainty estimation with deep learning. We find empirical support that method ( 5 ) coupled with a randomized prior function significantly outperforms ensemble-based approaches without prior mechanism. We also find that ( 5 ) significantly outperforms ( 4 ) in deep RL. We suggest a major factor in this comes down to the huge dimensionality of neural network weights, whereas the output policy or value is typically far smaller. In this case, it makes sense to enforce prior beliefs in the low dimensional space. Further, the initialization of neural network weights plays an important role in their generalization properties and optimization via stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [ 23 , 38 ] . As such, ( 5 ) may help to decouple the dual roles of initial weights as both ‘prior’ and training initializer. Algorithm 1 describes our approach applied to modern deep learning architectures.

C.5 Ensembles without priors

This paper builds upon a line of research that uses an ensemble of trained models to approximate a posterior distribution. Compared to previous works, our main contribution is to highlight the importance of a ‘prior’ mechanism in ensemble uncertainty. Figure 13 presents an extremely simple example of 1D regression with a (20,20)-MLP and rectified linear units. The data consists of x i = i − 5 5 x_{i}=\frac{i-5}{5} for i = 0 , . . , 10 i=0,..,10 and y i = 5 𝟙 { i = 10 } y_{i}=5\mathds{1}\{i=10\} .

The results above highlight the drawbacks of naive ensembles. A pure ensemble trained from random initializations fits the data exactly and leads to almost zero uncertainty anywhere in the space [ 31 ] . A bootstrapped ensemble takes the variability of the data into account and thus has a wide predictive uncertainty as x x grows large and positive. However, where the data has target value zero, bootstrapping will always produce a zero target and consequently the ensemble has almost zero predictive uncertainty as x x becomes large and negative [ 47 ] .

This lack of prior uncertainty can lead to arbitrarily poor decisions, as outlined in [ 50 ] . If an agent has only ever observed zero reward, then no amount of bootstrapping or ensembling will cause it to simulate positive rewards. This issue is easily remedied by the addition of a prior mechanism, either through l 2 l_{2} regularization to initial random weights ( 4 ), or the addition of a fixed additive random ‘prior network’ ( 5 ).
4 Deep reinforcement learning

Algorithm 1 might be applied to model or policy learning approaches, but this paper focuses on value learning. We apply Algorithm 1 to deep Q networks (DQN) [ 42 ] on a series of tasks designed to require good uncertainty estimates. We train an ensemble of K K networks { Q k } k = 1 K \{Q_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} in parallel, each on a perturbed version of the observed data ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} and each with a distinct random, but fixed, prior function p k p_{k} . Each episode, the agent selects j ∼ Unif ( [ 1 , . . , K ] ) j\sim{\rm Unif}([1,..,K]) and follows the greedy policy w.r.t. Q j Q_{j} for the duration of the episode. This algorithm is essentially bootstrapped DQN (BootDQN) except for the addition of the prior function p k p_{k} [ 47 ] . We use the statistical bootstrap rather than Gaussian noise ( 5 ) to implement a state-specific variance [ 19 ] .
